The insurance system is set up so that doesn't happen. There's something called reinsurance where companies will buy and sell risk from each other like it's a financial instrument to minimize their exposure to natural disasters. If insurance company A can sell a disproportionately large number of policies California but insurance company B sells a disproportionate number of policies in Oklahoma and Texas, then company A might go bankrupt if there are lots of wildfires and company B might go bankrupt if there are lots of tornadoes and hailstorms. Company A might and company B might sell insurance to each other against the risk of having to pay out huge amounts of money in the even that there are a lot of California wildfires or Oklahoma/Texas tornadoes and hailstorms. As I understand it, risk modeling is a big part of what insurance companies do, and the insurance regulators demand it and check up to make sure they're doing it, because insurance is such an important part of the financial system that if the risk is not properly managed, there's the potential that something like a fire that wipes out half of Chicago could act as a contagion that bankrupts multiple companies like dominoes the way that the collapse of investment banking companies almost did in 2008 when the mortgage backed securities bubble burst and the stock market crashed.

Furthermore the government plays a role in the insurance market by providing some forms of subsidies and safety nets in the case of massive catastrophic events. If a house built on the coast is worth $3 million dollars but would only be worth $1 million if it was built further inland, the property tax revenue on that additional $2 million of property value provides a lot of incentive for governmental bodies to provide the financial infrastructure and use their taxing power to find a way to make it work.
